newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico auctions assets in post-crisis bargain sale.
newsitem.headline: Mexico auctions assets in post-crisis bargain sale.

text.p: A bargain sale of bank assets following Mexico's 1995 financial crisis was due to get underway on Wednesday with up to 18 foreign and international participants gearing up for the first auction, the agency conducting the sale said.

Bankers Trust and Mexican brokerage GBM are jointly lead managing the sale of some 135 million pesos ($17.1 million) of the choicest bank assets, all secured and current commercial and industrial loans, which go under the hammer on Wednesday.

"Today is auction day. Up to the penultimate stage 18 groups took part. We still don't know how many will participate today but we hope there will be around 12," said Oscar Medina Mora, director of the VVA government agency selling off the assets, told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday morning.

"We hope to give the result by the 10th (tomorrow) at the latest, unless there are legal complications," he said. "We have selected credit of above average quality -- secured and with up-to-date payments."
Initially 150 million pesos ($19 million) were due to be auctioned but one debtor paid back 15 million pesos ($1.9 million) owed to its bank in an eleventh hour self-rescue effort, he said.
Some 28 local and foreign groups participated in the initial part of the process, including five fully foreign firms, and Medina said foreigners were still in the picture.

Mexico's VVA (Valuation and Sale of Assets) is the agency charged with selling off bank assets in government hands as a result of the country's 1995 financial crisis, triggered by the sharp December 1994 devaluation of the peso.
Thousands of debtors failed to keep up payments on these assets as interest rates skyrocketed and earnings tumbled.

Via its FOBAPROA bank bail-out fund, the government took over of the banks' distressed and current assets and charged VVA with recovering as much of their value as possible, mainly through high-profile auctions.
The Camino Real hotel chain is among the real estate assets up for grabs, while assets on sale include everything from business and property debt to cars and family jewelry.
Medina said that within the next two days it hoped to post details of the next sale -- a large Mexico City office building, which he declined to name on legal grounds.

VVA also has credits from some 540 large companies, each credit worth at least 50 million pesos ($6.33 million), in its sale portfolio. The agency hopes to start selling off at least one of these by the end of July.

By the end of March next year Medina said VVA aims to have sold off assets worth 15 billion pesos ($1.9 billion) of a total of 340 billion pesos ($43.2 billion) that FOBAPROA has on its books to sell.
"We have something of everthing -- short term, long term, secured, unsecured, current -- we have the whole spectrum of debt," he said.
"In some cases we will also be selling company shares, where the banks have transformed debt into equity," he said.
He denied recent talk that the bank's sale of real estate would damage an already depressed property market.
"In the last two years 15 times more property was sold in Mexico City alone than the total FOBAPROA has on its books," Medina said. "We won't have a big impact."
He said VVA's goal was to help bank assets controlled by FOBAPROA return to their full vigour.
"We're establishing a process by which we can reinject vitality into the relationship between creditors and debtors," he said.
((--Mexico City newsroom +525 728 7905)
